summary: IGMP is how IPv4 hosts tell neighboring multicast routers which groups they want to receive. Version 3 adds source filtering, so a host can ask for traffic only from, or excluding, specific source addresses. This internet-standard text obsoletes RFC 3376.

plainLanguage.summary: Internet Group Management Protocol version 3 (IGMPv3) lets an Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) system tell nearby multicast routers which groups and sources it wants. Routers use these reports to guide multicast forwarding on each attached network.

subtitle: How IPv4 systems report multicast groups and filter traffic by source address.

tldr.problem: Multicast routers need to know which groups have listeners and which source addresses those listeners want. Earlier IGMP versions did not support source filtering.
tldr.mechanism: IGMPv3 hosts report INCLUDE or EXCLUDE filters with source lists. Routers send Queries, hosts send Reports, and routers maintain group and source timers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9776 is Internet Standard 100, obsoletes RFC 3376, and updates RFC 2236. It retains compatibility with earlier IGMP versions.

sections.title: What IGMPv3 Adds
sections.content:
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) lets IPv4 hosts and routers report multicast group membership to neighboring multicast routers. IGMPv3 adds source filtering: a system can request traffic from listed sources only, or from every source except those listed.

This version supports Source-Specific Multicast and is designed to interoperate with IGMP versions 1 and 2. RFC 9776 revises RFC 3376 with clarifications and errata fixes and updates RFC 2236.
sections.plainLanguage: A system can join a multicast group and also say which senders it wants to hear from. IGMPv3 reports that choice to nearby multicast routers.

sections.title: INCLUDE and EXCLUDE Filters
sections.content:
The service interface records a filter mode and source list for each socket, interface, and multicast address. INCLUDE means receive packets only from listed sources. EXCLUDE means receive packets from all sources except those listed.

The system combines the requests from its sockets into one interface record per group. If any socket uses EXCLUDE, the interface uses EXCLUDE with a combined list; if all sockets use INCLUDE, the interface uses INCLUDE with the union of their lists.
sections.plainLanguage: INCLUDE names the senders a system wants; EXCLUDE names senders it does not want. The system combines the requests from local applications into one reportable choice for each group on an interface.

sections.title: Queries and Membership Reports
sections.content:
IGMP messages use IPv4 protocol number 2. IGMPv3 introduces Membership Query type 0x11 and Membership Report type 0x22. Reports are sent to 224.0.0.22 and contain one or more group records.

A Query can ask about all groups, one group, or one group and specific sources. A Report's group records describe current state, a filter-mode change, or a source-list change. IGMPv3 senders set the auxiliary-data length to zero because this version defines no auxiliary data.
sections.plainLanguage: A router sends a Query to ask what a system wants to receive. The system answers with a Report that lists groups and their source filters.

sections.title: How Group Members Respond
sections.content:
After a Query, a system waits for a random delay bounded by the Query's maximum response time before sending a Report. It can combine pending responses for the same interface or group. It must not send a Report immediately after a General Query.

When the interface's reception state changes, the system sends a State-Change Report immediately and retransmits it to help cover packet loss. The host does not suppress its report merely because it hears another member's report.
sections.plainLanguage: Systems wait a random amount of time before answering a Query so replies are spread out. A change in what they want to receive triggers an immediate report, which is repeated in case it was lost.

sections.title: How Multicast Routers Track Interest
sections.content:
A router keeps state for each group on each attached network, including a filter mode, a group timer, and source timers. It sends general Queries periodically and uses specific Queries to check whether listeners still want a group or source before pruning traffic.

IGMP supplies membership information to the multicast routing protocol; it does not override that protocol's routing information. If a lower-address router sends a General Query, the current querier stops sending its own general Queries.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers keep timers for groups and sources and ask again before stopping traffic. They use the membership reports as input to multicast routing, not as a replacement for routing information.

sections.title: Compatibility, Security, and Status
sections.content:
IGMPv3 systems must support compatibility modes for older queriers and group members. The RFC also notes that IGMP provides no confidentiality and discusses forged Queries and Reports that could alter router behavior or consume host resources.

RFC 9776 is Internet Standard 100. It obsoletes RFC 3376 and updates RFC 2236; the batch metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.
sections.plainLanguage: Newer systems can work with older IGMP systems by switching to a compatible mode. Messages can be forged on a network link, so the RFC describes checks and limits that reduce some risks.

viz.caption: THE SIX IGMPV3 GROUP RECORD TYPES

items.label: CHANGE_TO_INCLUDE_MODE
items.desc: Reports a change to INCLUDE mode.

items.label: CHANGE_TO_EXCLUDE_MODE
items.desc: Reports a change to EXCLUDE mode.

items.label: ALLOW_NEW_SOURCES
items.desc: Lists additional sources the system wants.

items.label: BLOCK_OLD_SOURCES
items.desc: Lists sources the system no longer wants.
